newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Indonesia's Medco takes Kazakh oil co stake.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Indonesia's Medco takes Kazakh oil co stake.

text.p: Indonesia's Central Asia Petroleum Ltd has bought a 60 percent stake in Kazakhstan's largest oil company Mangistaumunaigaz for $4.35 billion, a senior Kazakh minister said on Monday.
Most of the remaining shares will be floated off to portfolio investors, in what the government hopes will give a decisive push to a new Kazakh stock exchange.

Kazakhstan signed the contract on Sunday with Central Asia Petroleum, a subsidiary of PT Medco Energy Corp, a government statement said. Previous reports, including some on Reuters, had said Central Asia Petroleum was part of Indonesia's Sedtco group.

"The gist of the contract is as follows -- the company buys a 60 percent stake and pays $4.348 billion for it, $4.1 billion of which is its investment proper and $248 million of which is a bonus to the government," Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference.
Pavlov, who is chairman of Kazakhstan's tender committee, said the Indonesian company was chosen "because its offer was incomparably better than that of (six) other bidders".
Central Asia Petroleum must invest the $4.1 billion over 20 years, including $2 billion in the first five years, he said.
It will have to pay penalties if investments fall behind schedule, he said.

Another 10 percent of Mangistaumunaigaz will be owned by employees. The government will retain a 30 percent stake, which will eventually be sold off to portfolio investors on a stock market the former Soviet republic plans to set up by the year-end, he said.
The deal gives the Indonesian company a foothold in one of the world's most energy-rich areas, although it needs billions of dollars of investment to realise its potential.

"We have committed billions of dollars of our resources to this project and in cooperating with the government and employees of Mangistaumunaigaz we will do our best to make it the most successful venture in this country," said Hilmi Panigoro, head of Central Asian Petroleum.
"We commend the government of this country for creating an economic climate which is very conducive to attracting corporations like us to invest in this economy," Panigoro said.
He said his company was planning to at least double the production of crude oil of Mangistaumunaigaz over the next five years.
Mangistaumunaigaz is located in the West of the Central Asian state and is its largest oil company. Last year it produced only four million tonnes of oil.
In Soviet times oil production at Mangistaumunaigaz, which sits on reserves estimated at 200 million tonnes, peaked at 25 million tonnes which is equivalent to Kazakhstan's current annual oil output.
Pavlov said the government hoped that large foreign investment would revive the troubled oil industry and also maintain its social infrastructure, reduce unemployment and improve workers' skills.

"If this joint venture turned out to be a successful one, we are confident that more investors from Indonesia and other countries of the surrounding Asian region would come to this country," Panigoro said.
